questions.why: Extra points can be ignored or count against you.

questions.q: Skimming a text means
o: reading quickly for the general idea
questions.why: Scanning is looking for specific information.

questions.q: A question asks for one detail. What is best?
o: A short, precise answer taken from the text
questions.why: Read the question carefully: extra wrong details can cancel a right one.

long.q: Read the text and answer the questions. 'Community gardens are spreading in many cities. In Riverside, a group of neighbours turned an empty car park into a garden in 2019. Volunteers meet every Saturday morning to plant vegetables, and anything they grow is given free to a local food bank. Organiser Maya Patel says the biggest benefit is not the food but the friendships: "People who had lived on the same street for twenty years had never spoken before." The project now plans to add a small classroom so that local schools can visit.' (a) What was the site before it became a garden? (b) When do the volunteers meet? (c) What happens to the food they grow? (d) According to Maya Patel, what is the biggest benefit of the garden? (e) What does the project plan to do next?
scheme: B1: (a) an (empty) car park
B1: (b) (every) Saturday morning
B1: (c) it is given free to a (local) food bank
B1: (d) the friendships / neighbours getting to know each other (not 'the food')
B1: (e) add a (small) classroom (for school visits)
long.ans: a car park; Saturday mornings; given free to a food bank; the friendships; add a classroom

questions.q: Good notes are
o: brief points under the given headings
full sentences copied from the text
questions.why: Notes should be short and relevant to each heading.

questions.q: In note-making, what should notes be?
o: Full sentences copied from the text
Brief points under the headings given
questions.why: Each note should be a separate, relevant point.

questions.q: What is lost if two notes say the same thing?
o: The second note earns no extra mark
questions.why: Make every note a different point.

long.q: Read the text and make notes under two headings: 'Benefits of cycling to school' (two notes) and 'Problems' (two notes). 'More students at Greenhill School now cycle to school. Cycling is cheaper than taking the bus, and many students say they arrive feeling more awake. It also reduces traffic outside the school gates at 8 a.m. However, there are not enough bike racks, so some bicycles are left against walls, and parents worry about a busy road junction near the school. In winter, rain and dark mornings also put some students off.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a benefit: any of cheaper than the bus / arrive more awake / less traffic at the gates
B1: a second, different benefit from that list
B1: a problem: any of too few bike racks / busy junction (safety) / rain and dark winter mornings
B1: a second, different problem from that list

questions.q: A summary should be written
o: in your own words, as one paragraph within the word limit
questions.why: Continuous, concise prose is expected.

questions.q: What should a summary include?
o: The relevant points, in your own words and in the word limit
questions.why: Organise points logically.

questions.q: Why keep to the word limit?
o: Long summaries are penalised and lose focus
questions.why: Plan the points first.

long.q: Read the text, then write a summary of the benefits of part-time jobs for teenagers. Write about 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Many teenagers take part-time jobs while they are still at school. Earning their own money teaches them how to budget, and many say they value things more when they have paid for them themselves. Jobs in shops or cafés also build confidence, because young workers must speak to customers and solve problems quickly. Employers say that teenagers who have worked are often more reliable and punctual later in life. Some students also discover what kind of career they would like, or would not like, through these jobs. Critics point out, though, that working too many hours can leave students tired in lessons.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: they learn to budget / manage money
B1: they value things more when they have paid for them
B1: they gain confidence (dealing with customers, solving problems)
B1: they become more reliable and punctual
B1: they find out which careers they would (or would not) like
B1: own words, about 80 words, and no drawbacks included (tiredness is not a benefit)

questions.q: Which is the most suitable opening for an email to a friend?
questions.why: Informal register for a friend.

questions.q: Which tone suits an email to a friend?
questions.why: Match register to the reader.

questions.q: What must an informal email cover?
o: All three bullet points in the task
questions.why: Develop each point.

long.q: Write an email (120–160 words) to a friend about a school event you helped to organise: what it was, what you did, and what you would do differently. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: all three points covered and developed
B1: friendly, informal register throughout
B1: well organised, with an opening and closing
B1: a range of accurate grammar and vocabulary

questions.q: A report usually has
o: a title and clear sections or paragraphs with a recommendation
questions.why: Reports are organised for a reader to act on.

questions.q: Which phrase fits a formal register?
o: In my view, this proposal would benefit students.
questions.why: Formal writing avoids slang and contractions.

questions.q: Which is suitable for a report to a head teacher?
o: Formal language with clear headings or paragraphs
questions.why: Give recommendations where asked.

long.q: Your school wants to reduce plastic waste. Write a report for your headteacher (150–200 words) suggesting two ideas and recommending one. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a clear title and purpose
B1: two ideas, each explained with a benefit
B1: a reasoned recommendation
B1: formal register, no slang
B1: accurate, varied language

questions.q: In a gap-fill listening task, your answer should usually be
o: one or two words heard in the recording
questions.why: Write the words you hear, spelled correctly.

questions.q: In the listening exam, what should you do before the recording starts?
o: Read the questions and note what information is needed
questions.why: Spelling of key words still matters.

questions.q: Answers in the listening exam should be:
o: Brief, as instructed, with key words spelled recognisably
questions.why: Listen for the specific detail asked for.

long.q: Ask someone to read this aloud to you once while you don't look at it, then complete the notes with one or two words or a number. 'Hello everyone, and welcome to the Bayside Aquarium. Our tour today lasts about forty-five minutes. We'll start at the shark tunnel, which opened last year, and finish at the rock pool, where you can touch starfish. Please don't use flash photography, because it upsets the animals. The café is on the second floor and closes at four thirty. Finally, if you'd like to volunteer here, you must be at least sixteen.' Notes: Tour length: ___. First stop: ___. At the rock pool, visitors can touch ___. Not allowed: ___ photography. Café closes at ___. Minimum age for volunteers: ___. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (about) 45 minutes
B1: (the) shark tunnel
B1: starfish
B1: flash
B1: 4.30 / four thirty
B1: 16 / sixteen

questions.q: In the speaking test it helps to
o: develop answers with reasons and examples
questions.why: Extended, relevant answers score best.

questions.q: In the speaking test, what helps most?
o: Extending answers with reasons and examples
questions.why: Respond naturally to the examiner's prompts.

questions.q: If you don't understand a question in the speaking test, you should:
o: Ask politely for it to be repeated
questions.why: Asking for clarification is natural communication.

long.q: Record yourself speaking for 2–3 minutes on: 'Is it better to grow up in a city or in the countryside?' Talk about transport and facilities, friendships and free time, the environment, and say which you'd choose and why. Then listen back and mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: every prompt developed with reasons or examples, not one-line answers
B1: both sides considered before a clear choice
B1: a range of accurate grammar and topic vocabulary (facilities, commute, peaceful, isolated)
B1: clear pronunciation and keeps going without long pauses

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.

questions.q: 'Despite ___ tired, he finished the race.'
questions.why: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form.

questions.why: Reluctant means not wanting to do something.

long.q: Each sentence has one mistake. Rewrite it correctly. (a) She don't like coffee. (b) I have lived here since five years. (c) If I will see him, I will tell him. (d) He is more taller than his brother. (e) We discussed about the problem.

B1: (b) I have lived here for five years.
B1: (c) If I see him, I will tell him.
B1: (d) He is taller than his brother.
B1: (e) We discussed the problem.
